An early pregnancy termination can result in either a missed miscarriage or an induced abortion. A missed miscarriage, also known as a silent miscarriage, occurs when a pregnancy ends naturally, but the fetus has not been expelled from the uterus. The body may not show any symptoms, and the pregnancy may not be aware that the miscarriage has happened. The body may eventually expel the fetus, or a medical procedure may be required to remove it.

An induced abortion is a deliberate termination of a pregnancy, usually performed during the first trimester. The process involves removing the contents of the uterus, including the fetus and placenta, using medication or a surgical procedure. The specific methods and procedures may vary depending on the stage of the pregnancy, the patient's health, and the provider's recommendations.
reference_answers: An abortion is a procedure to end a pregnancy. It uses medicine or surgery to remove the embryo or fetus and placenta from the uterus. The procedure is done by a licensed health care professional. The decision to end a pregnancy is very personal. If you are thinking of having an abortion, most healthcare providers advise counseling.

Higher blood sugar levels cause more glucose to attach to hemoglobin, resulting in a higher A1C level. An A1C level of 6.5% or higher typically indicates diabetes, while an A1C between 5.7% and 6.4% suggests prediabetes. Lower A1C levels indicate better blood sugar control. Regular A1C testing is important for managing diabetes and reducing the risk of complications associated with the disease.

The test measures the average level of glucose (sugar) in your blood over the past 2-3 months by checking the amount of glycated hemoglobin in your red blood cells. Hemoglobin is a protein found inside your red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout your body. When sugar enters your bloodstream, some of it attaches to hemoglobin, forming glycated hemoglobin.

The more glucose there is in your blood, the higher the amount of glycated hemoglobin will be. It provides valuable information about overall trends rather than short-term fluctuations, allowing healthcare providers to evaluate the effectiveness of treatment plans and adjust them accordingly.

This test is different from the blood sugar checks that people with diabetes do every day. Your A1C test result is given in percentages.
